Title: Simulations of a new neutron imaging station at the CROCUS zero power reactor
Text:
Abstract — Neutron imaging (NI) complements X-ray 
radiography by exploiting the strong interaction of neutrons 
with several light elements and a high penetration for many 
heavy elements. Hitherto no dedicated NI beamline currently 
exists at the zero-power CROCUS reactor. Establishing such 
a station would create a low-cost platform for student 
training, materials R&D, and proof-of-principle studies that 
feed larger facilities. Using the Serpent 2 Monte Carlo 
neutron transport code, we explored how to modify an 
existing zero power research nuclear reactor into a useful 
neutron source for NI. Three measures proved decisive: (i) 
inserting a 70 mm-diameter air (or vacuum) tube through the 
300 mm water reflector, boosting channel flux by 
approximately factor of fifty (ii) retaining a thin water layer 
between fuel and tube to convert fast neutrons to thermal 
ones without excessive attenuation; and (iii) employing low-
scatter aluminum windows and vacuum flight tubes to 
preserve beam intensity   over source-to-detector ~5m 
distance. A resolution-versus-flux map identified an optimal 
layout that balances image sharpness and count rate for the 
detector planned for first radiographs in 2025. The outcomes 
of the simulations show that a reflector modification can 
deliver performance comparable to demonstrator stations at 
VR-1 in Czechia and AKR-2 in Germany, and they underline 
CROCUS’s potential as a national testbed for neutron 
radiography, and potentially even low-resolution computed 
tomography.  
Keywords —Neutron imaging, Zero-power reactor, Monte 
Carlo neutron transport. 
I. INTRODUCTION
ESEARCH reactors, particularly zero-power facilities,
play an important role in nuclear‐engineering education 
[1], code validation [2], and small-scale R&D [3], [4], [5], [6]. 
CROCUS, a 100 W water-moderated UO₂-Umetallic research 
reactor at EPFL, has served these functions since the early 
1980s [7]. To date it has been used mainly for pile oscillation 
measurements [8], benchmark experiments [7], detector testing 
[9], and hands-on training of hundreds of students and young 
professionals. Maintaining such reactors is increasingly 
challenging as budgets tighten and ageing facilities face 
shutdown; expanding their experimental portfolio is therefore 
essential for long-term sustainability [10]. Neutron imaging 
(NI) [11], a non-destructive radiographic technique sensitive to 
several light elements such as hydrogen, lithium or boron offers 
an attractive, modern use case. Upon this call, few facilities in 
Europe have started designing and running NI experiments such 
as the VR-1 zero power reactor in Czechia [12] and AKR-2 zero 
power reactor in Germany [13], [14]. Installing an NI beamline 
at CROCUS would (i) broaden the reactor’s academic impact 
by supporting experiments over a broad palette of scientific 
domains, such as materials science [15], cultural-heritage 
studies [16], and advanced fuel research [17]; (ii) provide a

complementing the high-flux spallation source SINQ [18]; and 
(iii) supply compelling justification for continued operation and
upgrades. This paper presents Monte Carlo simulations to
assess and optimize a practical NI station for the CROCUS
reactor, demonstrating that a reflector modification can provide
a useful thermal neutron flux and spatial resolution without
compromising reactor safety or usability. The design goals of
the NI setup are to maximize thermal neutron flux while
minimizing fast neutrons and gamma radiation, achieve a field
of view (FOV) of approximately 15 × 15 cm², maintain a
reasonable collimation ratio (L/D) suitable for industrial
applications, incorporate a variable aperture for flexibility, and
ensure the overall system is not complicated for the installation
and user-friendly for operation. The foreseen detector system is
based on a scintillator coupled with a CCD (Charge-Coupled
device) camera [19]. The structure of this paper is as follows:
Section II introduces the CROCUS zero-power research reactor
and the Serpent 2 Monte Carlo neutron transport code used in
this study. Section III outlines the steps taken to enable neutron
imaging at CROCUS, including proposed design modifications,
simulation results, and the final layout. Section IV summarizes
the findings and suggests directions for future development.
II. TOOLS AND MATERIAL
In this section, we present the characteristics of the zero-
power reactor CROCUS and the Monte Carlo neutron transport 
code Serpent 2 used to conduct the optimization in this study.

facility designed for educational and experimental use [2], [7],

CROCUS functions as a critical assembly using uranium fuel 
and light water as a moderator. The reactor features a 
concentric dual-zone core configuration, with uranium oxide 
fuel in the inner zone and metallic uranium fuel in the outer 
zone, as shown in Fig 1. CROCUS is instrumented with four 
main monitoring detectors: two compensated ionization 
chambers placed to the north and south of the core for general 
monitoring, and two east-west fission chambers calibrated for 
power measurements [20]. Additionally, the reactor supports 
various neutron detection systems, including 3He proportional 
counters and scintillation detectors [9]. The reactor’s diameter 
is 60 cm and has a height of one meter. 
Fig 1- (left) Isometric view of the CROCUS reactor vessel and its internal 
components.(right) Top grid of the reactor shown in detail. 
The reactor is enclosed in a 1.3 m thick concrete shielding 
structure, as shown in Fig 2 ,that serves as radiological 
protection during operation. However, a horizontal channel 
has been built into the shielding at the core’s mid-height, 
specifically for experimental purposes. This channel enables 
placing the neutron imaging detector outside the concrete 
shielding, taking advantage of the increased distance for better 
image formation. All subsequent calculations are performed 
along the axis of this experimental channel. 
Fig 2- Top view of the reactor cavity and shielding in the reactor hall; 
proposed detector location shown. 
B. Serpent 2 Monte Carlo neutron transport code
The Serpent 2 code [21], a Monte Carlo neutron transport code 
widely used in reactor physics and radiation shielding studies, 
was used in this work. In addition to its primary use for 
generating group cross-section libraries for diffusion codes, 
Serpent 2 can also predict kinetic parameters [22], includes 
variance reduction techniques [23], and has been validated for 
shielding applications [24]. These features make it a suitable 
candidate for modeling the CROCUS zero power reactor and 
performing calculations relevant for the implementation of 
neutron imaging within the CROCUS facility. 
III. ENABLING NEUTRON IMAGING IN CROCUS
In this section, we present the proposed modification to be 
implemented in the CROCUS reactor to achieve the best 
possible neutron imaging within the facility’s limitations. 
A. Channel within reflector
The reflector in the CROCUS reactor consists of 
approximately 300 mm of water, which significantly 
attenuates both thermal and fast neutrons. To increase the 
fraction of thermal neutrons passing through the experimental 
channel, an air-filled channel with an inner diameter of 70 mm 
was inserted into the reflector, as shown in Fig 3.  
Fig 3 - CROCUS model, horizontal cut at mid-height, in the Serpent 2 Monte 
Carlo code, featuring an air channel inserted into the reflector. 
Simulations were performed with several tallies placed at 
different distances from the core center, all located at the mid-
height of the reactor and aligned with the air channel in the 
reflector. Notably, this air channel is concentric with the 
experimental channel in the concrete shielding. A second 
simulation was conducted using the same tally positions but 
without the air channel. The results, shown in Fig 4, indicate a 
50-fold increase in neutron flux with the air channel in place,
highlighting the importance of this modification for
maximizing the flux outside the reactor vessel for neutron
imaging applications.

B. Material used inside the channel inside the reflector
To enhance the neutron flux exiting the core, specifically the 
thermal neutron component, we investigated replacing the air 
in the channel with polyethylene or heavy water. The goal was 
to assess whether these materials could improve 
thermalization of fast neutrons and thereby increase the 
thermal neutrons reaching the outside.  
Fig 5- Neutron spectra measured outside the reflector channel for different 
channel materials. The default configuration refers to the case with no channel 
present in the reflector. 
Several simulations were conducted using different materials 
within the reflector channel. A tally positioned 10 cm outside 
the channel was used to evaluate the resulting neutron 
spectrum for each case. As shown in Fig 5, air yields the 
highest thermal neutron flux. While heavy water improves 
thermalization of fast neutrons, it also scatters already 
thermalized neutrons, reducing overall thermal flux. The latter 
case is similar for polyethylene. Given the limited flux 
available in a zero-power reactor, air is the recommended 
material for the channel. Although a vacuum could further 
reduce scattering, it is not considered due to mechanical 
complexity. 
C. Gap between the fuel and the channel
Reactor cores with reflectors typically exhibit a peak in 
thermal neutron flux at the core–reflector interface [25]. By 
adjusting the gap between the air channel and the core, it may 
be possible to exploit this effect. As shown in Fig 6, the gap 
was modeled in Serpent 2 (S2), and several cases were 
simulated, starting with the channel in direct contact with the 
fuel and progressively increasing the distance. A tally was 
placed outside the channel to measure total, thermal, and fast 
neutron fluxes. Additionally, a tally, 10 cm outside the reactor 
in front of the channel, was included to monitor the reaction 
rate of  6Li, as the planned neutron imaging detector will use a 
6LiF:ZnS based scintillator. As illustrated in Fig 7, the thermal 
neutron flux remains relatively constant within the first 20 mm 
of gap distance before starting to decline. In contrast, the fast 
neutron flux decreases linearly as the gap increases. As the 
total flux is the sum of both components, it reflects a 
combination of these trends. The key performance metric is 
the ⁶Li reaction rate, which, as shown in Fig 8, remains stable 
within the first 20 mm, mirroring the thermal flux behavior. 
The observed variation falls within the statistical uncertainty 
of the Monte Carlo simulations. Considering mechanical 
constraints, a gap of 10 mm between the fuel and the channel 
is recommended as it preserves thermal flux while ensuring 
structural feasibility.

region and the channel.

D. Simulation of flight tubes
In this section, we investigate the effect of air on beam 
intensity, focusing on its impact on thermal and fast neutron 
flux. To simulate this, a 6 m-long, 10 cm-diameter cylinder—
matching the dimensions of the experimental setup—was 
modeled. The source energy spectrum was taken from the 
detailed CROCUS simulation at the exit of the reflector 
channel and placed at one end of the cylinder, with a neutron 
tally at the opposite end. The cylinder was filled with air 
containing water vapor at varying relative humidity levels. 
The uncertainties shown on the graphs are directly extracted 
from the tally information given by the Monte Carlo code. The 
first test examined how relative humidity affects neutron flux. 
As shown in Fig 9, no significant change was observed in 
total, thermal, or fast neutron flux. 
Fig 9 - Total, fast and thermal flux in function of the relative humidity of air. 
Next, we investigated the effect of air pressure on neutron 
flux. Reducing air pressure lowers air density, which in turn 
decreases the total macroscopic cross section. As shown in Fig 
10, a noticeable reduction in neutron flux occurs when the air 
pressure exceeds 100 mbar.
Fig 10 - Total, fast and thermal flux in function of the air pressure. 
Additionally, as shown in Fig 11, hydrogen contributes only a 
small fraction (10–16%) to the total macroscopic cross 
section. This explains why changes in humidity had little 
impact on neutron flux compared to variations in air pressure. 
Fig 11 - Relative contribution of each nuclide in air to the total macroscopic 
cross section for a relative humidity of 78%. 
For a zero-power reactor like CROCUS, a flux reduction of up 
to 20% is observed at ambient pressure compared to 50 mbar, 
as shown in Fig 10 . To mitigate this loss, aluminum flight 
tubes can be installed along the beam path, i.e., a tube from 
the exit of the reactor’s vessel until the camera’s field of view, 
allowing air to be passively or actively evacuated to maintain 
a pressure below 100 mbar.

IV. CONCLUSIONS
This paper presents Monte Carlo simulations aimed at 
assessing the feasibility of establishment of a neutron imaging 
beamline at the CROCUS zero power research reactor at 
EPFL, Switzerland. The proposed reflector modification, 
involving the insertion of a 70 mm-diameter air-filled channel 
through the reactor’s water reflector, which enhances thermal 
neutron flux at the imaging location by approximately factor 
of fifty. Air was identified as the optimal material for the 
channel, outperforming alternatives such as polyethylene and 
heavy water due to its minimal neutron scattering and 
absorption. A gap of 1 cm between the channel and the reactor 
fuel is recommended, balancing mechanical feasibility and 
maintaining high thermal neutron flux. 
Further flux improvement can be achieved by incorporating 
vacuum flight tubes at reduced pressure (~50 mbar), which 
decreases neutron scattering and boosts thermal neutron flux 
by an additional 20%. A practical NI design proposal is 
provided, incorporating these optimized features to ensure 
maximum neutron flux and appropriate image resolution for 
industrial and research applications. 
The findings underline the feasibility of implementing a 
dedicated neutron imaging station at CROCUS, promising a 
valuable national platform for training, materials research, and 
neutron imaging demonstrations. Future work will include the 
experimental validation of these simulations.

Abstract: Neutron imaging (NI) complements X-ray radiography by exploiting the strong interaction of neutrons with several light elements and a high penetration for many heavy elements. Hitherto no dedicated NI beamline currently exists at the zero-power CROCUS reactor. Establishing such a station would create a low-cost platform for student training, materials R&D, and proof-of-principle studies that feed larger facilities. Using the Serpent 2 Monte Carlo neutron transport code, we explored how to modify an existing zero power research nuclear reactor into a useful neutron source for NI. Three measures proved decisive: (i) inserting a 70 mm-diameter air (or vacuum) tube through the 300 mm water reflector, boosting channel flux by approximately factor of fifty (ii) retaining a thin water layer between fuel and tube to convert fast neutrons to thermal ones without excessive attenuation; and (iii) employing low- scatter aluminum windows and vacuum flight tubes to preserve beam intensity over source-to-detector ~5m distance. A resolution-versus-flux map identified an optimal layout that balances image sharpness and count rate for the detector planned for first radiographs in 2025. The outcomes of the simulations show that a reflector modification can deliver performance comparable to demonstrator stations at VR-1 in Czechia and AKR-2 in Germany, and they underline CROCUS’s potential as a national testbed for neutron radiography, and potentially even low-resolution computed tomography.
